title: Review: Osmosis and water potential; Active transport, bulk transport and co-transport; How enzymes work; Factors affecting enzyme activity
specRef: CC3(c), CC3-SP1, CC3-SP2; CC3(c); CC4(a), CC4(b), CC4(d), CC4(f); ...
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EZ01a#t4 term and clue written for the game; MB04#t2 term and clue written for the game; EZ01a#t2 term and clue written for the game; EZ01b#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EZ01a#N.10a, EZ01b#N.8b, EZ02#N.11a, MB03b#N.3, MB04#N.3a, EZ01a#N.11, EZ01b#N.6, EZ02#N.6a, EZ01a#N.2a, EZ01b#N.9, EZ02#N.3a, EZ02#N.8a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Specificity
items.clue: Property by which each enzyme acts on one reaction, or on a few very similar ones.

items.label: Respiratory inhibitor
items.clue: Substance that cuts a cell's ATP supply, so uptake against a gradient falls sharply.

items.label: Activation energy
items.clue: What is needed to break bonds in the substrate before it can react; an enzyme lowers it.

items.label: Lock and key
items.clue: Fischer's 1894 model: a rigid binding pocket that only an exactly complementary substrate fits.

questions.stem: Lipase catalyses the hydrolysis of triglycerides but has no effect on starch. What is the reason?

options.text: Starch molecules are too large to enter the active site, but any molecule smaller than starch could.
The active site of lipase is complementary in shape and chemical properties to a triglyceride only.
Starch requires more energy to break down than lipase is able to supply to the reaction.
Lipase seeks out triglyceride molecules in the fluid and ignores starch molecules it meets.

questions.explanation: Specificity arises from the structure of the active site: its shape and chemical properties match one substrate, so starch cannot bind in a way that allows catalysis.

questions.stem: Trypsin is made by cells in the pancreas and digests proteins in the small intestine. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Trypsin is extracellular because it is made outside cells, in the pancreatic juice.
Trypsin is intracellular because proteins are digested inside the cells lining the small intestine.
Trypsin is extracellular: it is made inside pancreatic cells, secreted, and acts in the small intestine.
Trypsin is intracellular because it is made inside cells, like every enzyme.

questions.explanation: Made inside cells, secreted by exocytosis, acting outside cells: that is an extracellular enzyme.

questions.stem: At high substrate concentrations, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction levels off even when more substrate is added. Why?

options.text: The enzyme molecules have been used up by the reaction, so no more product can be formed.
Every active site is occupied almost all the time, so extra substrate finds no free site to bind.
The high concentration of substrate denatures the enzyme, so its active site stops working.
The amount of energy the enzyme can supply each second has reached its upper limit.

questions.explanation: At saturation, as soon as one product leaves an active site another substrate binds. Adding substrate cannot increase the frequency of productive collisions further.

questions.stem: A plant cell has a solute potential of −700 kPa and a pressure potential of +200 kPa. What is its water potential?

options.text: −500 kPa
−900 kPa
−700 kPa
+500 kPa

questions.explanation: ψ = ψs + ψp = (−700) + (+200) = −500 kPa. The positive pressure potential raises the water potential above the solute potential.

questions.stem: Root cells absorb nitrate ions from soil water in which the nitrate concentration is much lower than in the cell. When the roots are deprived of oxygen, nitrate uptake falls sharply. What explains these observations?

options.text: Nitrate is taken up by active transport in the same direction as diffusion but faster, and the lack of oxygen slows the diffusion.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP from aerobic respiration, so without oxygen the supply of ATP falls and active transport slows.
Nitrate is taken up by pumps using ATP already present in the cell, so removing oxygen must have affected the channel proteins instead.
Nitrate is taken up by facilitated diffusion through channels, which use ATP to move ions across against the gradient.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical bacterium, enzyme E catalyses the conversion of compound A to compound B. The conversion of A to B releases energy. A mutation stops the bacterium from making enzyme E. No other enzyme in the bacterium acts on compound A. Which prediction about compound B in the mutant bacterium is best supported?

options.text: B no longer forms at all, as A cannot change into B without enzyme E.
B forms at the normal rate, as the bacterium makes a new enzyme because it needs B.
B forms at the normal rate, as ATP supplies the energy that enzyme E used to supply.
B still forms, but far more slowly, as the reaction is no longer catalysed.

questions.stem: According to the induced-fit model, what happens when a substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme?

options.text: Both the enzyme and the substrate change shape as they bind.
The rigid active site admits only an exactly matching substrate.
The active site closes around a substrate that keeps its shape.
The enzyme seizes the substrate and holds it without any changes.

questions.explanation: Both change shape when binding occurs. The closer fit strains bonds within the substrate, which is part of how catalysis is achieved.

questions.stem: A student measured the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction at six temperatures. The rates, in arbitrary units, were: 10 °C, 2; 20 °C, 4; 30 °C, 8; 40 °C, 15; 50 °C, 9; 60 °C, 1 (illustrative data). Which conclusion is supported by these data?

options.text: The low rate at 10 °C shows that the enzyme had been denatured by the cold temperature.
The true optimum is 37 °C, the body temperature at which every enzyme works at its best.
The optimum is near 40 °C; above it, denaturation outweighs the faster collisions.
The fall in rate after 40 °C shows that the substrate had been used up at higher temperatures.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how an enzyme acts as a catalyst in a cell?

options.text: It is converted into product along with the substrate, so the cell must keep making it.
It makes possible a reaction that could not take place at all in its absence in the cell.
It transfers energy to the substrate so that the reaction is driven forward faster.
It increases the rate of a reaction that could occur without it, and is released unchanged.

questions.explanation: Enzymes are catalysts: they increase the rate of reactions that would otherwise occur far too slowly at cell temperature, and each molecule catalyses the reaction repeatedly.

questions.stem: Hexokinase is the enzyme that adds a phosphate group to glucose. X-ray structures show that the two halves of the enzyme are further apart when no glucose is bound. When glucose binds, the two halves close around it. What does this evidence show?

options.text: It supports the lock-and-key model, as glucose fits an active site of fixed shape.
It shows that glucose denatures hexokinase, because the shape of the enzyme changes.
It shows the lock-and-key model was worthless, as it explained nothing about enzymes.
It supports the induced-fit model: the active site changes shape as substrate binds.

questions.stem: Catalase was added to hydrogen peroxide and the volume of oxygen collected was recorded: 0 s, 0 cm³; 20 s, 12 cm³; 40 s, 20 cm³; 60 s, 24 cm³ (illustrative data). What is the best estimate of the initial rate of reaction from these data?

options.text: 0.4 cm³ s⁻¹
20 seconds
0.60 cm³ s⁻¹

questions.explanation: 12 cm³ of oxygen in the first 20 s gives 12 ÷ 20 = 0.60 cm³ s⁻¹. With readings every 20 s, this first-interval rate is the best estimate the data allow.

questions.stem: Pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2. When it passes with food into the small intestine, where the pH is about 8, its activity falls almost to zero. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The change in pH alters charges on amino acids, disrupting bonds that hold the active site's shape.
The alkaline conditions hydrolyse the peptide bonds of pepsin, breaking it up into free amino acids.
Pepsin has run out of substrate, because protein digestion is completed inside the stomach.
At pH 8 the enzyme and substrate molecules move more slowly, so they collide less often.
